what_its_for: Hydromorphone is a strong opioid pain medicine used to treat moderate to severe pain that other pain medicines have not helped enough. It works in your brain and nervous system to change how your body feels and responds to pain.
how_to_take: Take hydromorphone exactly as your doctor prescribes. Swallow tablets or extended-release tablets whole — do not crush, chew, break, or dissolve them, as this can release too much medicine at once and be very dangerous or even life-threatening. You can take it with or without food. If you use the liquid form, measure your dose carefully with the measuring device provided — never use a regular kitchen spoon. Do not take more doses or take it more often than prescribed.
dosing: Your doctor will set the right dose for you based on your pain level, medical condition, and how your body responds to the medicine. Doses vary widely from person to person. For regular tablets, doses are usually taken every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Extended-release tablets are taken once every 24 hours. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and you are taking this medicine on a regular schedule, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are taking it only as needed for pain, take it when you need it for pain.
storage: Store hydromorphone at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep it in a secure location that is out of reach of children, teenagers, and anyone else who should not have access to it. Do not store unused or leftover medicine for long periods. Dispose of unused medicine properly by using a drug take-back program or mixing it with an undesirable substance like coffee grounds or dirt, sealing it in a bag, and throwing it in the trash. Do not flush it unless the label or your pharmacist specifically says to.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking hydromorphone — combining them can cause dangerous breathing problems or even death. Avoid taking other medicines that make you sleepy, such as sleeping pills, anti-anxiety medicines, muscle relaxers, or other opioids, unless your doctor approves. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do activities that require full alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice as it may interact with some formulations. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: very slow, shallow, or stopped breathing; extreme sleepiness or trouble waking up; confusion or unusual behavior; blue or purple color on your lips or fingertips (signs of low oxygen); chest pain or a fast or irregular heartbeat; severe dizziness or fainting; seizures; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat. Also call your doctor if your pain is not well controlled, if you feel you need more medicine than prescribed, or if you experience signs of withdrawal such as restlessness, sweating, muscle aches, or nausea.
when_it_works: Hydromorphone usually starts working within 15 to 30 minutes after taking an immediate-release tablet or liquid. The effects typically last 4 to 6 hours. The extended-release form works more slowly and provides steady pain relief over 24 hours. This medicine helps manage pain but may not take it away completely. It works best as part of a complete pain management plan discussed with your doctor.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the effects of this medicine, especially dizziness and confusion. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Children: This medicine is generally not recommended for children unless specifically prescribed by a specialist. Pregnancy: Do not take this medicine during pregnancy unless your doctor has determined the benefits outweigh the risks. Babies born to mothers who used opioids regularly may experience withdrawal symptoms after birth. Breastfeeding: This medicine passes into breast milk and may harm a nursing baby — talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if your kidneys or liver do not work well, as the medicine can build up to dangerous levels in your body.
